questions.text: Which of the following is the most appropriate title for the passage?
questions.context: Software companies once assumed that disclosing a discovered security flaw only after a fix was fully ready protected users, since attackers would never learn of the vulnerability until it was already patched. Security researchers who track actual attacker behaviour complicate this assumption considerably: attackers frequently discover the same vulnerabilities independently, sometimes months before a company's own patch is ready, meaning delayed disclosure protects users only against the company's own timeline, not against attackers operating on a completely separate one. Some companies have shifted toward coordinated disclosure with a fixed deadline, forcing a patch to ship on a predictable schedule rather than whenever convenient, precisely because the old assumption left users exposed for however long the company happened to take.

options.text: Why Companies Should Never Disclose a Security Flaw Publicly
Why Delayed Disclosure Protects Against a Company's Own Timeline, Not an Attacker's
A History of Software Security Practices
Why Attackers Never Discover Vulnerabilities Independently
How Security Researchers Are Trained to Find Vulnerabilities

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: Two neighbouring countries that establish a formal interchange of goods along a shared border are often assumed to benefit roughly equally from the resulting trade, since both sides gain access to products previously unavailable or expensive to import. Economists studying specific border interchange agreements complicate this assumption: the actual distribution of benefit depends heavily on which side possesses the scarcer resource, since a country supplying a good the other side cannot easily substitute captures a disproportionate share of the trade's overall value, meaning formally equal access to an interchange rarely translates into an equally shared economic benefit.

options.text: the legal process required to formally establish a trade agreement
how formally equal trade access does not guarantee an equally shared economic benefit between two countries
the total volume of goods exchanged along a specific border annually
why some countries refuse to establish border trade agreements at all
a comparison of two specific countries' border trade policies

questions.text: Choose the most appropriate topic of the passage.
questions.context: A detective investigating a robbery who focuses resources on obtaining a suspect's confession rather than gathering independent physical evidence is sometimes assumed to be taking a shortcut around genuine investigative work. Legal scholars studying wrongful conviction cases complicate this assumption in the opposite direction: confessions obtained under prolonged interrogation pressure prove unreliable often enough that some jurisdictions now require independent corroborating evidence before a confession alone can support a conviction, meaning a detective who pursues physical evidence even after obtaining a confession is not being redundant, but is instead correcting for a documented weakness in confession evidence that a confession-focused approach alone cannot resolve.

options.text: the interrogation techniques permitted under current criminal procedure
how pursuing physical evidence even after a confession corrects for a documented weakness in confession reliability
the total number of wrongful convictions overturned annually
why some jurisdictions have abolished confession evidence entirely
a comparison of two specific jurisdictions' interrogation procedures

questions.text: Which of the following best states the main point of the passage?
questions.context: A novel's foreshadowing is often assumed to work by planting an explicit clue the reader consciously notices and later recalls once the foreshadowed event occurs. Literary researchers studying reader recall patterns complicate this assumption: the most effective foreshadowing frequently registers only subconsciously on a first reading, an unremarkable detail the reader does not consciously flag at all, and its effectiveness lies precisely in that initial invisibility, since a reader who consciously notices an obvious clue often feels manipulated rather than satisfied once the foreshadowed event actually occurs.

options.text: Effective foreshadowing always requires the reader to consciously notice an explicit clue.
The most effective foreshadowing may work precisely by registering subconsciously rather than consciously.
Readers always feel satisfied when they consciously notice an obvious foreshadowing clue.
Foreshadowing has no measurable effect on how satisfying a reader finds a novel's ending.
Literary researchers agree that foreshadowing should always be made explicit to readers.

questions.text: How many of the statements below do NOT agree with the passage?
questions.context:
I spent my first year renting a spacious but poorly maintained apartment convinced my landlord was simply neglectful, since every request I submitted seemed to disappear into silence for weeks at a time. It wasn't until another tenant in the building mentioned, almost in passing, that the landlord managed the property entirely alone while working a full-time job elsewhere, that I understood the silence had never been indifference, only genuine overload. I started submitting requests through a shared online form the landlord had actually set up months earlier but never mentioned clearly, and my repairs began arriving within days rather than weeks. I still feel a flicker of embarrassment that I spent a year assuming the worst about someone who was, in hindsight, simply overwhelmed rather than uncaring.

(b) Every repair request the writer submitted was addressed within days from the very beginning.
(c) Another tenant mentioned the landlord managed the property alone while working full time elsewhere.
(d) The landlord had set up an online request form but had never mentioned it clearly.
(e) The writer's repairs began arriving faster once she used the online form.
(f) The writer now believes the landlord was genuinely uncaring rather than overwhelmed.

questions.text: Which statement does NOT agree with the two explanations given in the passage?
questions.context: Employees who voluntarily disclose their own workplace mistakes to a manager, rather than waiting to be caught, are sometimes rewarded with lighter consequences than employees whose identical mistakes are discovered independently, a pattern two competing explanations attempt to account for. One explanation holds that voluntary disclosure genuinely signals trustworthy character, evidence a manager can reasonably weigh favourably when deciding how to respond. A second, competing explanation instead proposes that voluntary disclosure simply arrives before the mistake's full consequences have compounded, meaning the lighter response reflects a smaller, more manageable problem rather than any genuine judgement about the employee's character at all.

options.text: The first explanation attributes lighter consequences to voluntary disclosure genuinely signalling trustworthy character.
The first explanation suggests a manager can reasonably weigh this signal favourably.
The second explanation claims voluntary disclosure always arrives after the mistake's consequences have fully compounded.
The second explanation attributes lighter consequences to a smaller, more manageable problem rather than character judgement.
Both explanations attempt to account for the same pattern of lighter consequences following voluntary disclosure.

questions.text: Which of the following questions CANNOT be answered from the passage?
questions.context: Naval commanders in earlier centuries sometimes ordered a vessel to fly a false flag, disguising its true national origin, to approach an enemy vessel without triggering an immediate defensive response. This tactic carried genuine risk: international maritime convention generally prohibited actually firing upon an enemy while still flying a false flag, meaning a commander had to formally raise the true flag before engaging, a brief but critical window during which the element of surprise the disguise had created was immediately lost. Naval historians studying this tactic's actual battle outcomes found it succeeded often enough to remain in regular use for centuries, despite this built-in limitation, primarily because a genuinely confused enemy rarely reorganised its defences quickly enough within that brief window to fully counteract the surprise.
